title: Nosing Whisky Properly | Craft Beer School
desc: How to nose whisky properly: the right glass, distance, strength and water, plus a routine that gets past the alcohol to the real aromas.
teaser: Most people sniff whisky like a fire alarm. Here is the slow, deliberate way blenders do it.
standfirst: Most of what we call taste in whisky is really smell. Nosing badly gives you a blast of alcohol and little else. Nosing well gives you fruit, grain, wood and smoke in layers. Here is a routine that works.
sections: Most of the flavour is in the nose

Your tongue picks up sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. Everything else you call flavour, from vanilla to smoke to green apple, comes from aroma compounds reaching the smell receptors high in the nose. Some arrive through the nostrils when you sniff. Others travel up from the back of the mouth when you sip.

That is why a bad cold flattens every drink. It is also why nosing comes first in any serious tasting. Our guide to whisky tasting for beginners covers the full routine. This guide focuses on the nose.
Use a glass that gathers aroma

A tulip shaped glass with a wide bowl and a narrower rim is the standard tool. The bowl gives the whisky surface area to release aroma. The rim gathers it towards your nose. A copita, a small stemmed sherry glass, works the same way and is still used by many blenders.

A heavy straight sided tumbler is the worst choice for nosing. The aroma escapes before it reaches you. A wine glass will do if nothing else is to hand. Whatever you use, rinse it with water, never detergent residue. Let it dry. A trace of soap will mask delicate notes.

Alcohol vapour is the first thing out of the glass and it numbs the nose. So do not plunge in. Hold the glass at chest height and slowly bring it up. Stop when you first notice aroma, often 5 to 10 cm below your nose. Then move a little closer.

Take short, gentle sniffs rather than one long inhale. Some tasters keep the mouth slightly open, which lets some of the alcohol vapour pass through the mouth instead. Try each nostril separately. Many people find one is more sensitive than the other.

Rest between sniffs. Smell fatigue sets in within a few seconds of the same aroma. Look away, breathe normal air, then return.
Lower the strength to hear more

At 40% ABV and above, alcohol dominates. Professional blenders often dilute samples to around 20% ABV for nosing, because at that strength the alcohol steps back and the aromas come forward.

At home you do not need a lab. Add water drop by drop with a pipette or straw. Nose after each addition. With most whiskies you will notice a point where fruit, flowers or cereal suddenly appear. Our guide to adding water to whisky explains why: some aroma compounds are held in the alcohol and released when it is diluted.

Use still, room temperature water with little flavour of its own. Heavily chlorinated tap water will show up in the glass.

Aroma compounds evaporate faster in a warm glass. In an Indian room at 30 °C, a whisky releases alcohol quickly and can smell hot and sharp. In a cold room it can seem closed.

Aim for a room around 20 to 25 °C if you can. Pour just before nosing. Cover the glass with a coaster or watch glass between sniffs to trap the aroma. Avoid ice for a nosing session: it closes the whisky down and dilutes it unevenly.
What a good nose is actually doing

Experienced noses are not born with more receptors. They have learned to pay attention, to name what they smell and to remember it. Most people can detect far more than they can describe. The gap is vocabulary and memory, not biology.

That is why professional sensory panels train together with reference standards. A panellist smells a known compound, learns its name, then finds it in a real sample. The same approach works at home with kitchen ingredients. A brewer training on beer faults uses exactly the same method, with spiked samples of diacetyl or acetaldehyde, so the skill carries across drinks.

Use the same order every time so your notes are comparable:

  1. Nose neat from a distance, then closer. Write first impressions.
  2. Swirl gently, wait 10 seconds and nose again.
  3. Add a few drops of water, swirl and nose a third time.
  4. After tasting, nose the empty glass. Wood, smoke and heavier notes often linger there.

Write broad families first: fruity, floral, cereal, woody, smoky, sulphury. Then try to narrow each down. Fruity becomes citrus becomes lemon peel. An aroma wheel helps with the vocabulary.

Drink water through the session, keep pours small and never drink and drive.

Your nose improves with practice against real references. Put a vanilla pod, a piece of orange peel, a clove and some toasted bread in separate small jars. Smell each, then nose a whisky and look for them. Your first step tonight: do this with one whisky and one jar. Matching a smell in the glass to a smell you can name is how every trained nose starts.
faqs: What glass is best for nosing whisky?
A tulip shaped glass with a wide bowl and narrower rim, or a copita. Avoid straight sided tumblers.
Should I add water before nosing whisky?
Nose it neat first, then add water drop by drop. Many whiskies release more aroma once diluted.
Why does whisky burn my nose?
Alcohol vapour numbs the nose. Hold the glass further away, take short sniffs and dilute with a little water.
How far should I hold the glass?
Start at chest height and bring it slowly up. Stop when you first smell aroma, often a few centimetres below your nose.
